title: Destination Perpetuity | Craig O'Rourke | Talks at Google
description:
Author, investor and real estate professional Craig O'Rourke shares his fresh, direct and common sense approach to real estate investing. In this powerful Google Talk, Craig explains his theory of why intelligent real estate investing is by far the best way to build true wealth in today's complex and often confusing investor marketplace. Craig explains how to create a personal cash flow of annuity by building a portfolio of self-funding, self-sustaining income producing real estate.

Get the book here: https://goo.gl/ef6JGx
summary: Analyzed. No investable claims were extracted.

CRAIG O'ROURKE: So the first 20 years the building was paid off. AUDIENCE: OK. Your numbers aren't correlating to that timeframe? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Oh, they didn't? I have to go back and look. AUDIENCE: Oh, no. I'm wondering. I was confirming. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Oh, OK. Yeah. I know. Those slides, I've got to clean them up. They always confuse people. And it goes too fast too. So the first 20 years the building got paid off. And that's a good rule of thumb for anybody investing in real estate. You should really try and create a plan that pays your building off in 20 years. I'm looking at some very young people here. You pay your building off in 20 years when you're my age, you have that cash flow building. That's sort of the idea of it. And then the next 20 years you still have taxes, and insurance, and all of that. But because of the magic of inflation, those dollars are always big enough to then sustain extra cash flow for the investor. AUDIENCE: Got it. Thank you. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yep. Anybody else? AUDIENCE: Hello. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Hi. AUDIENCE: So obviously California's super expensive. If you want to buy anywhere in LA, It's basically $1 million, which is a couple hundred thousand down for a down payment. So even if you split it with a couple people, it's expensive. What are your thoughts on buying an investment property in another state, even if you're not there to kind of manage it? CRAIG O'ROURKE: That's a great question. So keep this in mind. That same argument you have right there was what people were having 40 years ago. And they'll be having 40 years from now. So you can buy in other states. You can buy in other parts of LA or other parts of Southern California. Risk equals reward. And when I work with clients, and they want to buy income producing property, I always ask them the same thing. I always say, what do you want? Do you want cash flow, or do you want to grow equity? And what do you think they always say? Both. That's what everybody wants, right? But you do have to make choices. In other words, we're in Venice right now. So if we go to buy an income producing property in Venice, our cap rate's probably going to be about maybe 2% or 3%. Right? It's really bad. It's going to take you forever to cash flow on a property like that. But what was our appreciation rate in Venice last year? It's like 8%. It's crazy, right? So now if we take those same dollars, and I'll give you a perfect example. I have a client that I sold his property in Redondo Beach. And he wanted to re-invest in Southern California. And the cap rates were not good. They were like 5% or 6%. And he said, you know Craig, I'm going to take my money and move it to Ohio. I can get a 9% cap, 10% cap. That's basically your rate of return on the money, right. And I said, OK. But he was young. He was 38, 39 years old. I said, but are you sure you want to do that? He said, why? He said, I have owned buildings there for years and they cash flow great. And I said, how do they appreciate? He goes, they don't. That's where you make your money. So you have to create a plan. You have to say, what do I really want out of this? So looking in these, if everybody here came to me and said, I want to invest some dollars, I'd say appreciation dollars first, and then cash flow dollars. So we have this beautiful thing called the 1031 tax exchange. So what I do with clients when they come to me early on in their 20s or 30s, like that, even in your 40s, my idea of a good plan would be to invest someplace that's appreciating. Don't worry about the cash flow yet. Let it appreciate. Get those appreciation dollars. Because that's where you make your real money in real estate. Then when you have those appreciation dollars, you do a 1031 tax exchange, which means the IRS allows you to, not sell that building, but trade that building for another property. So in other words, your taxes are deferred. There's no tax dollars coming out of your pocket until you would ever sell it. You take all of that equity. And you move it into another property that has a better cap rate. I did that with some clients just a few years ago. I started working with them almost 20 years ago. And we built this beautiful appreciation portfolio in the South Bay, Manhattan Beach, Hermosa Beach, Redondo Beach. And they bought all these properties. And for 20 years they just let them grow in appreciation. Didn't really have any money coming in that they could put in their pocket. The tenants funded all the bills. But then when they were ready to retire in their late 40s, we sold everything. We moved everything down to Long Beach. And their cap rate tripled. And suddenly they had six figures a year to retire off of. So you have to plan it out. AUDIENCE: OK. Thanks. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Anybody else? Yes. Good shot. Wow. AUDIENCE: Not a very good catch, though. Do you think there's any value to flipping houses, buying houses that are not good, or buying empty land and then developing them? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. Well, there's two different questions. One's developing and one's flipping. This is a tough market for flipping. You're about eight years too late. But we cycle through those markets all the time. And there are deals out there. I just worked with a developer recently. A year ago I found him a property that he could flip. And we're just working with counteroffers right now. But he's a very shrewd developer. He knows exactly what he's doing. He's got a crew. And he's going to make a couple hundred thousand dollars off it. But those deals are very hard to find at the moment. But we do cycle through those deals. Developing is different also. Developers have to look at properties. They have to put on their own developer glasses and look two to three years out, depending on what you're selling, what you're trying to build. And then you have to guess what the market will be like when you go to sell it. What will interest rates be like? What will our economy be like? So, again, seven, eight years ago it was easier to see this steamroller. Now, I personally think that we're in a very good economy right now. I personally think our economy is on a-- I think we're going to do nothing but grow right now. But with that growth comes higher interest rates too. Right? So it's a double edged sword, isn't it? So anybody thinking about buying, do it today, because you're never going to see these interest rates again. So even if you think prices are too high, don't worry about it, because when you buy real estate, whether it's income producing real estate, or real estate you live in, what you have to realize is, you're not buying real estate. You're buying a payment. And when you buy a payment attached to interest rates like today, it doesn't matter if the real estate goes like this. As long as you're buying it with a 10 year plan, you'll be fine. So don't ever buy real estate with short term plans like flipping, because that's how you can get burned. I'm very conservative. The safest way to buy real estate-- My theory is never sell anything, by the way. But that doesn't mean you can't trade it, do a 1031, or something like that. And I never buy anything with less than a 10 year plan. AUDIENCE: OK. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Personally. Anybody else? Yeah. Go. AUDIENCE: What do you think about for people that currently rent? Should you be prioritizing buying a place to live in, or should the investment idea kind of be parallel to where you're living? Because it's hard to save for a down payment to live, and to do this investment. CRAIG O'ROURKE: That's a good question. That's a lifestyle question. It's also a tax question. I would probably say to you, buy a place to live in if you like where you're going to be. If you know you're going to be here at Google for a while, and you're stable in your job, and you're stable in your community, buy a place to live, because the tax write offs for your personal residence are going to outweigh the tax write offs for an investment property. And what you can do when you go to sell that property, or better yet, trade that property, you can then move that equity into an income producing property if you want. So you can do that. But in Venice and other areas of LA right now, the average renter, if you have 20% down, you can buy and own for less than you can rent when you figure all your tax savings and your deductions. So if you're renting right now and you can afford to buy, buy it, because these interest rates, we'll never see them again. Anybody else? AUDIENCE: Yeah. So I have two questions. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Sure. AUDIENCE: The first one is simpler maybe. In terms of your credentials, why don't you just brag about your own portfolio and how this has helped you? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Well, yeah. I mean, it's great. I will. I'll brag about that. [LAUGHTER] And I'll also tell you what I did wrong. So here's my story. I started investing when I was in my early 20s. And by the time I got to 44 or so, I was retired. I was done. I had all the positive cash flow I needed to retire. And then I started seeing these investments that looked really good. A little bit too good maybe? And one by one I started selling properties off and investing in these other investments. It turned out to be a Ponzi scheme. I lost almost everything. And by the time I was 50 I had to start over. 58, next month, right back where I needed to be. I had great focus, and it was my career, so it was not hard for me to do. I did have a little bit of real estate that I was able to play with and move things around. And I knew how to watch the market and see where to go. But I've done it twice. It works. AUDIENCE: Thank you. And then the second question is, is your advice to people-- and maybe you already answered this, so forgive me, but is your advice to people who don't have that much cash to partner with other people? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. I talk about that in my book. Talk about double edged swords again. They're good and they're bad. You have to really be careful who you partner with. And even if it's your best friend, or a sibling, or whatever, get everything in writing. And most importantly, get a good exit strategy in writing. Because invariably, if you two guys partner on something, one of you is going to want out before the other one. And it's going to be a problem. So you have to create an exit strategy. You have to do all that. But it is one of the best ways to own real estate. And I've owned I don't even know how many pieces of property. And I've owned dozens and dozens of properties in partnerships. And just you have to be careful who you partner with. And you have to be very clear on who's doing what, and how you're getting out. And then partnerships are fine. Yeah. Yes. AUDIENCE: I bought management companies. I've heard stories, good stories and bad stories. Like oh, we'll take away all your headache. And then some of it is like, oh my god, if I've done it myself it would have been better, save me way more money. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. AUDIENCE: Any? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. It's management-- [SIGHS] Yeah. AUDIENCE: Because if you have so many properties you're going to have management for sure. CRAIG O'ROURKE: I know. AUDIENCE: Do it yourself. CRAIG O'ROURKE: So we have seven properties, my family and I. And we have some we manage ourselves, some we have property managers for. It's like anything else. It's hard to find good property managers. So if you're going to invest in income producing real estate, I would almost find a good property manager first. And the best way to do that is talk to people that you know that own income producing real estate. Ask them who they use. Get references. Get referrals. Go online. Check everybody out. There's some really good people out there. And you shouldn't have to pay more than about 5% or 6% for a really good property manager. And I will tell you this, if you get a good property manager, they'll actually make you more money. Because what they do is they are going to keep your units filled. They're going to keep them filled at market rent. If there's a problem, they're going to take care of it, not you. So property management is the way to go. But you have to be very careful who you choose as your property manager. Yes? AUDIENCE: I'm curious to hear how the new tax laws are affecting 1031 exchanges and write offs. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. Well, there's no effect with 1031s. But write offs, depreciation is a big deal. That's a big, big deal. So what's happening is that your primary residence is now capped at $800,000. So that's going to be a game changer for real estate. Now, I live in Redondo Beach. So our neighboring community is Manhattan Beach. And the joke there is everybody lives in a McMansion, right? They're these giant houses, 3,500, 4,000 square feet. The yard's about as big as this stage. And everybody moved in there 25 years ago. And they were really popular. And everybody paid like $1 million or $2 million for them. Well, now they're worth about $2.5 million in today's market, right? But my crystal ball says, people aren't going to want those. Because, first of all, they're all filled with empty nesters. They don't want to go up and down those stairs anymore. And the house is too big. They're going to try and sell them. And guess what. If I'm going to buy a house, I'm not going to buy a $2.5 million giant box that I can only write off maybe a third of my interest. So that portion of the market is really going to be impacted. Now, I would say that the $1.4 million and less market-- good luck finding something like that anywhere around here-- but that market's going to be very solid. So the real estate community is going to change. And, as all of that's going on with these new tax laws, mark my words, interest rates are going up this year big time. So with the new incoming Fed chief, you're probably going to see at least three raises this year, if not more. And I think they'll be significant. They're not going to be Janet Yellen raises. They're going to be real raises. So we're going to be in a shifting economy. So if I was planning on buying something, what would I buy today? I'd try and probably look for a primary residence. If I didn't have only 20% to put down, I'd probably look for something at $1.4 million, $1.3 million, something like that to maximize as much of that $800,000 as I could. But I'd get in the interest rate game right now. Because that's going to change. AUDIENCE: Thank you. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Anybody else? Yes. AUDIENCE: I was wondering, if you were to choose an investment, would you prefer, assuming they are the same price range, single family, versus multi unit, versus a condo in a complex? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. Great question. And I'll take those in order of what I believe to be the least desirable. And that's the condo. Condo is least desirable because when markets shift they always get hurt the worst. You have the least control over a condo, and the least control of your finances because you also have an association that's controlling how much you have to spend every single month. And the desirability of resale is much less than a single family. So condos are the least desirable. Single family is in the middle. Single family is great. Always going to have a single family market. People love those. They always appreciate really well. But the multi-family will do better as an investment always. Why? It's because what we call the number of doors. So doors refers to how many tenants you have. So if you have a single family home over here, and you have a three unit building over here, and you have a vacancy over here, you got a 100% vacancy. If you got a vacancy over here, you have a 1/3 vacancy. And everything, your costs always get so much-- the words are escaping me here. There's a cost benefit basically to having multiple units. And you'll always, always do better. Investors look for as many doors as they can. So somebody who's really a big time investor in the multi-family, they want a huge complex. They want as many doors as they can, because that's really where you make your money is the number of doors, the number of tenants you have. And that's the safest way to go as well. Anybody else? AUDIENCE: I have a question. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yes. AUDIENCE: So I was wondering if you had any thoughts on commercial versus residential real estate, and basically if there's different strategies that you need to take with each? And what are the things to caution about? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Sure. Risk equals reward. And it's interesting. I own commercial properties. And we also own residential income producing properties. The commercial properties, a few years ago when the economy melted down, what happened? What happened? The stock market failed. Real estate prices plummeted, and businesses shuttered down, right? So there went your commercial real estate. What happened to multi-family? Bulletproof. As a matter of fact, so many people lost their homes, there was such a big pool of renters, prices went up. When was the last time you heard rents are going down? It just doesn't happen. Residential income producing real estate, in my book I talk about it being recession resilient. I wanted to put recession proof, but my publisher said I couldn't do that. I'd get sued. But recession resilient. I believe it's recession proof if you buy in the right area. When was the last time you heard rents are going down? It doesn't happen. But with commercial, it does. Commercial goes through that. Plus with commercial, like I own a couple of warehouses. And both of them I've split into two pieces. They were single, but I put two tenants in there just to mitigate in case one moves out. But I've had both of those dark at times. Now, I get a much better rate of return, a much better cap rate, if you will, off of my commercial properties. But I don't lose any sleep off my residential income properties, especially if I have a good property manager. Anybody else? AUDIENCE: For someone who wants to get into or add real estate as part of their portfolio, but does not want to do anything with buying, management property, et cetera, is there an easy way where I can just give my cash to someone and get some of a return? I mean, there's REITs, but peer to peer stuff. Do you have a recommendation for someone? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. Give it to me. I'll take care of it. No. REITs are fine. But keep in mind, when you own REITs, you don't own real estate. You own stock. That's different. So there are groups that do that. And, again, it's kind of like the property management question. It's like, who are you giving your money to? I've just seen too many people hurt on those. Personally I think if you're going to be a real estate investor, and there is work to it, and there's work the entire time you own it, I think you have to be hands on, or probably then just buy a single family home. And that is your real estate nest egg. AUDIENCE: Actually my question was exactly why not just buy like that fund in our 401k? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Exactly. That's stocks. That's REITs. But you don't have as much control over that. And you have a different set of write offs. So you can certainly invest in real estate that way. But when you invest with a portfolio like that, somebody else is making those bigger choices for you. You're deciding when to buy and when to sell, right? But what is invested in is different. And there's a cost to that. Because those people that run the REITs are getting paid. So there's a large amount of what could be your profit that's going to them. So if you make those choices yourself, you're gaining all that profit yourself. It's just a different theory of investing. AUDIENCE: Cool. Thanks. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. Yes. AUDIENCE: Hi. Do you have any tips for market research except looking at cap rates? Like other things that you would look at? CRAIG O'ROURKE: My tip is get a good real estate agent. Seriously. I mean, that's my best tip is find somebody who's a professional in the area you want to look at. AUDIENCE: No. I mean, like research for areas. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Oh, research for areas. You know, that's a good question. And that's a fluid question too, because areas are always gentrifying. Like right now everybody's excited about Inglewood. The stadium's going in there. What's going to happen with Inglewood. And people are excited about Hawthorne too. Is SpaceX going to buy the Toyota space and move in there? So there's all these sort of fluid things going on. Right now in Southern California we're in such a good market I think that you're fine almost wherever you go. But look at anybody that bought real estate 15 years ago in Venice. My gosh, right? Just unbelievable. So you see something happening like Google moving into a neighborhood, put money there. There's all kinds of things like that. So you have to watch for the opportunities. And you just have to be cognizant of what's going on around you. Anybody else? AUDIENCE: So I have a question. So basically if you have two options, one is a really nice house on a smaller piece of land, versus a crappy house on a large piece of land. So if you wanted to choose between the two, what is the trade off? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Buy the crappy one. Always. Always. You always want to buy the worst house in the best neighborhood. Location, location, location. Those are truly the three rules of real estate. And if you're a handy guy, and you can get in there and fix it yourself, or you have the money, that's a great opportunity. Because that property, if somebody's selling it in a condition like that where it's falling apart, it's been priced accordingly, or you're going to pay for it accordingly. And then you create what you want it to be. You go in, and you decide what floors you want, and countertops, and all that. You make it your own, especially if you're going to live there. And even if you're going to rent it out, you do the same thing. But you'll always want to buy, if you have the time, and the energy, and the willpower to go through all that. Because it's a lot. But it's like with somebody else asked about property management. Real estate you'll always be involved in maintaining that to some level, even if you have property managers. So if you're not scared of that, if you're not scared of taking that property and making it something better, that's the opportunity. Yes. AUDIENCE: So this might be an open ended question on your advice for looking for tenants if I don't have a management firm. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Oh. AUDIENCE: Like how long the contract is, and what do you look for in a tenant if you're doing that? CRAIG O'ROURKE: The first thing you do is run a credit report. And what I always do, I run a credit report, and I tell my prospective tenant, here's a credit report. You pay for it. If you have A plus credit, I'll rent the place to you and pay for your credit report. But if your credit's bad, and I give him a break point, then you're paying for the credit report and I'm not renting it to you. And what happens then is most people who have bad credit don't even run the credit report. They just go away on their own. So once you get the credit report, that's really what you're looking at, because people that have good credit, they got there by paying their bills. And that's really what you're looking for. AUDIENCE: Hi. CRAIG O'ROURKE: Hi. AUDIENCE: So if you were to be looking at an investment property, like let's say a fourplex, and you're OK with it maybe being like a long term investment, like 10 years plus, you're going to kind of be more focused on the long term appreciation and keeping hold of it, what would be a sort of minimum cap rate that you would recommend purchasing at? And also do you want something that perhaps needs a little bit of work, so as tenants move out you can kind of come in and do a little bit of cosmetic fixing? Do you want something that you don't have to do anything to? Not even like cosmetic that has no vacancies, and has a really low turnover? CRAIG O'ROURKE: You have a lot of questions. OK. AUDIENCE: Yeah. Sorry. CRAIG O'ROURKE: That's all right. AUDIENCE: That was like five questions. CRAIG O'ROURKE: I think I got them all. OK. So let's start with the cap rate, because that's really important. Cap rates are area specific. And they're also property specific. So like we said earlier, cap rate here in Venice is probably about 2 and 1/2%, 3%, something like that. Cap rate down in Long Beach is about 6 and 1/2%. So, again, I would say, what is your motivation? Are you buying for appreciation or are you buying for cash flow? If you say I want both, then I'm going to find an area with about 5% cap rate. So that's the cap rate thing. There's no right cap rate or a wrong cap rate. There's a right cap rate and a wrong cap rate for a specific area. And also for a specific property too. Because even if you're in Long Beach, and you have one property that has an ocean view and another one that's next to a smelting factory, they look exactly the same, they're going to have different cap rates because they're different desirabilities. So those questions are always very specific. Each property is so specific. But right now, in general, most of my investors are looking for a 5% cap. And that's not that easy to find. And so that's sort of the hard part is finding that middle of the road property. And that's where most investor dollars are going. Your other question. Remind me? AUDIENCE: It was, do you want to buy something that maybe needs a little bit of light cosmetic work, so that as a tenant moves out you can do a little work and increase the rents? CRAIG O'ROURKE: Yeah. Again, risk equals reward. If you don't mind doing that, you'll get a property that probably will be on the market for a little bit less money. And when they move out, as long as you have sort of that slush fund going, and you're willing to spend those dollars. Because when they move out you will need to spend those dollars. You will need to paint. You will need to carpet. You will need to bring it up to whatever the level is of that rental market. So you have to really keep those dollars on hand. And depending on what the property is, depending on the value of the property, it's healthy to keep a pretty handy slush fund around, because you never know. If all of a sudden three or four people go dark at once in a 10 unit building, that's a lot of money going away. So you have to be prepared. Not only do you have to keep your mortgage going, right? Your taxes, your insurance, all that. But now you've got to rehab all these units. It usually doesn't happen like that. Usually people move out one at a time. Usually they're giving you notice. Usually it's lot more smooth. But you never know. AUDIENCE: Right. Thank you. [CLAPPING]
